title: Create Account: Domain Account
summary: Domain account creation is the persistence variant where the intruder adds an account to the central directory rather than to a single host, so one credential unlocks every system and service that trusts that domain. With enough rights, the command that adds a user in Active Directory Domain Services can be run against the domain controller, which produces a directory object with organisation wide reach. The advantage for the attacker is scale and cover: the new account authenticates normally on any domain joined machine, can be placed in groups that grant administrative rights across many hosts, and does not require software to be installed anywhere. The directory records the creation with metadata that the attacker cannot easily forge, including the creating account, the originating workstation and a timestamp, and that creation is followed by a first logon and by group membership changes. Detection therefore starts with the directory audit trail and with the change control record: every new domain account should trace to a request, and any account created outside change windows or by an unexpected administrator is the priority review.

beginner.definition: A domain account is a user account kept in a central directory that many computers trust. This sub-technique is when an attacker creates one of these central accounts so they can log in to many systems. It is different from a local account, which exists on one machine only.
beginner.whyItMatters: One domain account can reach far more than a single computer. If it is given administrative group membership, the attacker controls the whole environment from one login. The account looks like any other user in the directory. Detection depends on checking the audit trail of the directory against the list of approved changes.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains rights that allow changes to the central directory, which is Active Directory.
A command such as net user add with the domain option creates the new account.
The account is stored on a domain controller, meaning the server that holds the directory.
Group membership may then be added so the account can administer many computers.
The attacker logs in from any joined machine and reaches shared services.
The directory records who created the account, when, and from which workstation.
beginner.example: Picture a large office building where a single badge works in every department. A worker in the badge office adds a new name to the central system and prints a badge for it. Now the badge opens the finance floor, the server room and the car park. No locks were changed and every door log shows a normal entry.
takeaways: A domain account is more powerful than a local one because it reaches every trusted system.
Directory audit records show who created an account, when and from which machine.
Compare every new domain account against an approved change request.

objectives: Explain what an Active Directory domain account is and how it differs from a local account.
Describe the rights an attacker needs before creating a domain account.
Identify the directory audit fields recorded when an account is created.
Explain why domain accounts are more valuable for persistence than local accounts.
Describe how change management records help separate valid accounts from attacker ones.
